facts: Pa'rus is a Southern Paiute word that means tumbling water, referring to the Virgin River alongside the trail.
The Pa'rus Trail is the only trail in Zion National Park that allows both bicycles and pets on leashes.
Running the Pa'rus Trail gives you a smooth, paved path with mostly flat terrain perfect for a gentle warmup.
Zion's famous towering canyon walls are made of Navajo Sandstone, sculpted over millions of years by water and wind.
Utah's first national park was originally declared Mukuntuweap National Monument in 1909 before being renamed Zion.
Angels Landing is one of the park's most famous rock formations, named because only an angel could land there.
Keep an eye out for desert bighorn sheep gracefully navigating the steep rocky cliffs around the canyon.
The Narrows is the narrowest section of Zion Canyon, featuring towering walls a thousand feet tall above the river.
Zion provides a vital sanctuary for the rare California condor, one of the world's largest flying birds.
The Virgin River continues to carve Zion Canyon deeper by cutting through bedrock as it flows downhill.
Water seeping out of sandstone walls creates lush hanging gardens of ferns and wildflowers right in the desert.
Checkerboard Mesa displays a unique crisscross pattern etched into sandstone by horizontal bedding and vertical cracks.
Ancestral Puebloans and Fremont people inhabited the Zion region long before it became a national park.
The valley floor sits at around 4,000 feet above sea level, offering a nice mild altitude challenge for runners.
The Great White Throne is a massive white sandstone monolith that dominates the view along Zion Canyon.
Zion features four distinct life zones, housing hundreds of species of mammals, birds, reptiles, and native plants.
Local Utah honey and freshly baked bumbleberry pie are popular treats for hungry athletes visiting the canyon towns.
The annual Zion Half Marathon brings runners from around the world to race near the park's majestic borders.
Zion National Park is an officially designated International Dark Sky Park, offering breathtaking views of the stars at night.
Water dripping from the alcove of Weeping Rock takes over twelve hundred years to travel through the sandstone.
